job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Sam Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at seven and on the 7:50 bus to a small civil engineering firm on the edge of Leeds. I'm a junior design technician, so most of my day is checking drainage drawings against the council's rules and fixing the red marks my senior, Marguerite, leaves on them. I passed my degree without any placement year, so honestly I still feel like I'm catching up. I share a flat with my mate Dan, and Friday lunch is the best bit because the whole office goes to the chip shop.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was getting the job like, and how does the work feel so far?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The job came through my dad's union friend, who knew the firm needed a junior, and I interviewed twice. Pay is good for my age and Mum and Dad said they'd back me if I ever ran short, so money isn't what keeps me awake. What bothers me is that half of what I check is the same dull rule-matching every week, and I've seen the senior staff trying software that does it for them. I haven't touched any of that. I like doing it by hand because I understand what I'm looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, nothing to see. Marguerite (my senior) has been through three waves of new software and the drainage rules are still the drainage rules. At the pub I'd tell my mates the hype was a way to sell subscriptions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be relieved, because I'm slow with new tools and I'd rather get properly good at the job I have. I still worry that my firm cuts a junior anyway to look modern. Cheap software gives bosses an excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now and try to get my chartership paperwork started early. I'd put about 300 pounds a month into my savings, since my parents' backing means I can. I'd also go to the union branch meeting my dad keeps pushing, because I think workers should be at the table whichever way it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's the world I trained for, and my family have steady jobs. There's a small knot about being the junior who never touches the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you like doing the checking by hand. Does anything about your day change if the software gets a bit faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. The tools save Marguerite maybe an hour on a big drawing, and a quick check of that can be handed to me. So my days might get a little more of the boring part and less of the thinking. I'd still be fine, but I'd say it out loud to her if I found myself only doing button-pushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell at work if you felt things were being rushed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marguerite first, since she signs off my work and listens. Then the union rep at my dad's depot, who has seen firms try this before. I wouldn't go to the director, because a junior does not do that.

say: I'd say the **hype** is mostly selling subscriptions and the drainage rules still stay the drainage rules.
I'd tell friends my job is **steady** and the firm is still hiring.
think: I'm relieved, because I'm **slow** with new tools and want to get properly good at what I do.
I still worry a firm could cut a junior just to look **modern**.
do: Carry on checking drawings by hand and start my **chartership** paperwork early.
Put **300 pounds** a month into savings, because my parents' backing lets me.
Go to the **union** branch meeting my dad keeps suggesting.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a small knot about being the junior who never learns the new tools.
S0.quote: I'm slow with new tools and I'd rather get properly good at the job I have.
fieldNote: He is secure and says so, but his **resistance** to tools is already a quiet worry.
Trusts unions and his dad's network more than employers.
Said 'between us' that a cheap tool gives bosses an excuse to cut juniors.

steps.text: Start the chartership paperwork with Marguerite this winter
Move 300 pounds a month into a savings account
Go to the union branch meeting at my dad's depot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving faster than the people in charge admit, and the juniors are the ones who pay first. Firms save money by not hiring us and then complain nobody has experience. That's what I'd say online too, and loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is in the first line. Checking drawings against rules is exactly the thinking task they say AI takes over. If Marguerite's firm halves the number of checkers, I'm the newest and cheapest to let go, even if it looks bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a training day on whatever tool they pick, even though it makes my stomach turn, because being left out is worse. I'd go to every union meeting and push for a rule that any job cut gets six months' notice. I'd also quietly apply to the water company's own team, as public bodies tend to cut slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got money behind me, and my parents, but my career hasn't started yet and it already feels shaky. It feels unfair that nobody voted for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather not chase new tools. How would you handle a target that assumes you use them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My manager has hinted at a target of 'two more drawings a day with the new software'. If that comes, I'd say yes, then ask in writing whether it changes my review. Dan's mate lost a contract role that way last spring, and it stuck with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which colleagues would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth, the older technician two desks down. He is 58, has never touched the software, and the firm will find it easy to say he's too slow. I'd stick up for him in a meeting, but I'm also the one who could be replaced by what he's worried about.

say: I'd say **juniors** pay first, because firms stop hiring us and then complain nobody has experience.
I'd say it **loudly** online that cuts need six months' notice.
think: Checking drawings against rules is **exactly** what AI takes first, so I'm in the line of fire.
The newest and cheapest worker is the easy **cut**, and that's me.
do: Ask for a **training day** on whatever tool the firm picks, even though I dislike it.
Push the union for **six months'** notice on any cut.
Apply quietly to the water company's own team, as **public** bodies cut slower.
feel: **Anxious**, because my career hasn't started and already feels shaky.
S1.quote: Firms save money by not hiring us and then complain nobody has experience.
fieldNote: Concrete fear: a **target** of two more drawings a day.
Blames firms and absent regulation, not the technology.
Worries for Gareth (58) more than for himself, then admits he is also exposed.

steps.text: Ask my manager for a training day on the new checking software
Push the union branch for six months' notice on cuts
Apply to the water company's design team
Write to my MP asking for rules on AI job cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments are asleep and this needs a public response now: a jobs guarantee, regulation and maybe a shorter week. I'd say it to my MP, my dad's union and anyone who'll listen. Private companies won't slow down on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my degree is worth nothing by 2028. Two years isn't enough time for me to retrain into anything, and I'm not fast at learning anyway. If the thinking part of design goes, the site work stays about three years longer, but I never did site work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the chartership plan straight away, because it would take four years and the profession might not exist. I'd save every pound and talk to Dad about whether his depot has openings, because buses and engineers on the road last longer. I'd also join a march, my first ever, and ask the firm what its plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. I've been sleeping badly just thinking about it. I'm 22 and picturing my whole career gone before I've paid for a sofa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what changes about the plan you just gave me for the next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go from 300 a month saved to about 900, which is nearly all my pay after rent. I'd also stop the planned Spain trip with Dan. If the firm cuts me, I have enough savings and Mum and Dad's spare room for about a year, and I'd be ashamed to need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your family would you turn to first, and for what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad first, because he's been through bus privatisation and knows how union fights go. He'd say it's time to organise. Mum would say come home and eat. I'd listen to both, but I'd say the main thing is I don't want to be the only one in the family who goes backwards.

say: I'd demand a **jobs guarantee** and rules for AI now, from my MP and my dad's union.
I'd say private companies will not slow down on their **own**.
think: My degree could be **worthless** by 2028, and two years is too short for me to retrain.
I never did site work, so I'm **exposed** on both counts.
do: Drop the **chartership** plan and save around 900 pounds a month.
Cancel the **Spain** trip and talk to Dad about openings at his depot.
Join my first **march** and ask the firm what its plan is.
feel: **Alarmed**, sleeping badly, and ashamed I might need my parents' spare room.
S2.quote: I'm 22 and picturing my whole career gone before I've paid for a sofa.
fieldNote: Resistance to change makes the **short** timeline feel worse.
Strong savings and family backing are real, but he feels shame about using them.
Turns to **collective** action first and to his father's experience.

steps.text: Stop the chartership application and save 900 pounds a month
Cancel the Spain trip with Dan
Ask Dad about openings at his bus depot
Join the union march and ask the firm for its plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to build the safety net properly, so let's use it. I'd say the same to my union rep and online: demand retraining paid for by the companies who profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be nervous but not frozen. Five years gets me to 27, and I could do a conversion course in something hands-on, like electrical installation. The thinking part of my job goes first, but the hands-on side gets about three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd keep my job and keep saving. In the first year I'd take an evening course in site safety and surveying, because that's close to what I know. I'd also ask Dad's union to lobby for a retraining fund, and I'd go with him to the meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix. There's a bit of fear, though also some relief that there's a runway. I'd feel better if the plan came from the public side and not just whatever the firm decides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a retraining grant that pays my rent while I study, because I can't live on savings and study at once, even with my parents' help. And I'd want firms to publish how many jobs they plan to automate. If they know, they should say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you most afraid of in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be scared Dan and I drift apart if I move for a course, since we've shared a flat for two years. I'd also be scared of ending up in a half-career with a surveying certificate and nowhere to use it. But that's a smaller fear than having nothing.

say: Five years is time to build a **safety net**, so demand retraining paid by the profit-makers.
I'd say firms should **publish** how many jobs they plan to automate.
think: I'm nervous but not frozen, since five years gets me to **27** with room to retrain.
The hands-on part of building gets about three more years, which is **breathing** space.
do: Keep the job and keep **saving** this winter.
Take an evening course in **site safety** and surveying in the first year.
Go with Dad to the union meeting about a **retraining** fund.
feel: Some **fear** but also relief that there's a runway.
Better if the plan comes from the **public** side.
S3.quote: I can't live on savings and study at once, even with my parents' help.
fieldNote: Has a **route**: site safety, surveying and electrical work are near what he knows.
Wants the state to carry the **risk** of retraining, not him.
Fear of ending in a half-career is realistic for a slow adopter.

steps.text: Sign up for an evening site safety and surveying course
Keep the job and save 300 pounds a month
Go to the union meeting about a retraining fund
Email my MP to ask for a paid retraining grant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a generation's job to get ready: schools, retraining and new rules. I'd say let's not repeat what happened to mining towns, when nobody planned. I'd put that in a union motion if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels almost comfortable, which is odd for me. By 32 I could have retrained twice. My worry isn't losing the job tomorrow, it's that I'll spend a decade watching and still be the person who hasn't learned the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and get chartered, since the rules and sign-offs probably stay human for longer. I'd start using one AI tool at work, one only, to see what it does. I'd also put a deposit together with my girlfriend Lena for a small flat, because buying while I'm paid well feels sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish, but with a nag. It doesn't feel urgent. I know that's the danger: slow people like me can sit on a decade and end up in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cousin starting a degree now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't skip the maths and don't skip the site visits. Learn to read a drawing and see why a rule exists. A tool can only do what you can check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your plans outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, family plans change. Lena and I would probably wait a few years for children, not for fear, but to see where the jobs land. I'd keep the savings anyway. A decade isn't a promise.

say: I'd say getting ready is a **generation's** job and we shouldn't repeat what happened to mining towns.
I'd tell younger people to keep the **maths** and site visits.
think: Ten years feels almost **comfortable**, but I could waste it and still be behind.
Rules and sign-offs probably stay **human** longer than drawing work.
do: Get **chartered** while the profession still values it.
Try **one** AI tool at work to see what it actually does.
Save a **deposit** with Lena for a small flat while I'm paid well.
feel: **Calm** on the surface, with a nag that slow people end up in a hurry.
S4.quote: Slow people like me can sit on a decade and end up in a hurry.
fieldNote: Self-aware about his **resistance**, which is the real risk he names.
Plans a flat deposit and delays children, which shows him thinking long term.
Trusts public bodies and **unions** over firms to manage the transition.

steps.text: Finish the chartership exams within three years
Try one AI drawing-check tool at work for a month
Put a flat deposit together with Lena

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, by far. I'd have no time to find a new path, and my slowness would hurt me the most. What would help is a public jobs guarantee, six months' notice on cuts and a retraining grant that pays rent. I'd also want my firm to tell juniors the truth about the plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as anti-technology as I sound. I just don't like being told I have to be quick. If someone showed me one tool, patiently, I'd probably use it.

headlineQuote: Two years isn't enough time for me to retrain into anything, and I'm not fast at learning anyway.
portrait: Sam is **22**, a junior drainage design technician in Leeds, who passed civil engineering with no placement year.
Strong savings and a family safety net keep him steady, but he is **slow** with new tools and never uses AI.
He leans left, trusts **unions** and public help, and blames firms and absent rules rather than the technology.
His mood climbs from calm in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in the 2-year picture, then eases with more time.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years leaves no time for a **slow** learner to start again.
whatWouldHelp: A **jobs guarantee**, six months' notice on cuts and a retraining grant that covers his rent.
